difficultyReason: Strengthen by confirming a load-bearing assumption about drug mechanism. Trap (A) sounds supportive but merely describes correlation; trap (D) strengthens a neighboring claim about a different patient group.
stimulus: A recent clinical trial found that patients with chronic migraines who took the new drug theralin reported, on average, four fewer migraine days per month than patients who took a placebo. Theralin blocks a neuropeptide that researchers have long suspected of triggering vascular inflammation in the brain. The trial's lead investigator concluded that theralin probably reduces migraine frequency by suppressing this vascular inflammation.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients who experienced the greatest reduction in migraine days also reported fewer headaches overall during the trial period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The manufacturer of theralin funded the clinical trial as part of its application for regulatory approval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theralin has been approved to treat several inflammatory conditions unrelated to the central nervous system.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who suffer episodic rather than chronic migraines also report fewer migraine days when taking drugs that target neuropeptides.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Brain imaging of trial participants taking theralin showed markedly lower levels of vascular inflammation than imaging of those taking the placebo.

explanations.correct: The investigator's causal story has two links: theralin suppresses vascular inflammation, and that suppression is what reduces migraines. (E) directly confirms the first link with imaging evidence, making the inflammation mechanism substantially more plausible.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — fewer headaches is a near-restatement of fewer migraines and doesn't speak to the inflammation mechanism.
explanations.B: If anything, weakens by raising a conflict-of-interest concern.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — approval for unrelated inflammatory conditions doesn't establish that theralin reduces brain inflammation or that such reduction is what prevents migraines.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about episodic migraine patients, not the chronic-migraine group the investigator's claim concerns.
explanations.E: Correct.

difficultyReason: Closes an analogical gap between two policy regimes. Trap (C) introduces an unwarranted comparison to a third jurisdiction; trap (E) is an alternative-cause distractor disguised as support.
stimulus: Ethicist: When the city of Vellmar imposed a small fee on single-use plastic bags at grocery stores, consumption of such bags fell by nearly 80 percent within a year. Our city council is now considering a similar fee. Critics claim the fee would be ineffective here because our residents are more affluent than Vellmar's and less sensitive to small charges. But the critics are mistaken: the fee will probably reduce plastic bag consumption in our city too.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city council is also considering a ban on single-use plastic straws at restaurants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vellmar also ran a public-awareness campaign about ocean pollution shortly before imposing the fee.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A neighboring city with a larger economy than the ethicist's imposed a similar fee and saw consumption fall by over 90 percent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grocery stores in Vellmar donated part of the bag-fee revenue to local environmental charities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In Vellmar, the reduction in bag use was greatest among the city's wealthiest residents.

explanations.correct: The critics' objection is that affluent residents are insensitive to small charges. (E) directly undermines that premise by showing the wealthiest in Vellmar actually responded the most, closing the analogical gap between the two cities.
explanations.A: Irrelevant — plastic straws are a separate policy and don't bear on whether the bag fee will work.
explanations.B: Introduces an alternative cause — the awareness campaign, not the fee, may have driven Vellmar's drop.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — the neighboring city introduces a new variable (larger economy) and doesn't address the affluence objection.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative cause — the charitable donation could explain Vellmar's reduction, weakening the analogy rather than strengthening it.
explanations.E: Correct.

difficultyReason: Rules out a prominent alternative cause in an economic argument. Trap (D) strengthens a sister claim about wages rather than hiring; trap (A) is the opposite answer, concessive to the alternative.
stimulus: When the minimum wage in the state of Karell rose from $12 to $15 last year, critics predicted significant job losses in the restaurant industry. But restaurant employment in Karell actually grew by 3 percent over the same period. Economists have therefore concluded that moderate minimum-wage increases probably do not cause the hiring reductions critics feared.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most supports the economists' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In years immediately preceding the wage increase, restaurant employment in Karell had been declining slightly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restaurant employment grew even more sharply in states that raised their minimum wage by similar amounts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Karell's overall economy experienced no unusual growth in the year the minimum wage rose.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The average hourly wage at Karell restaurants, including tips, rose by more than the minimum-wage increase alone would predict.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A few large restaurant chains closed locations in Karell during the year of the wage increase.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that Karell's economy was booming and masked what would otherwise have been job losses. (C) rules out that alternative by showing no unusual growth, so the minimum-wage increase is more plausibly responsible for the stable hiring.
explanations.A: Opposite answer — prior declines suggest there should have been further declines absent the wage increase, making the reversal harder to attribute to the wage change's neutrality.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison — other states' experiences don't by themselves rule out Karell-specific confounds.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about wage dynamics, not about hiring effects.
explanations.E: If anything, weakens, by suggesting some employment contraction did occur.

difficultyReason: Bolsters an unstated premise linking recidivism to a specific program feature. Trap (B) is accurate but irrelevant; trap (E) strengthens a different conclusion about a dissimilar population.
stimulus: The Kessington County jail began allowing inmates awaiting trial to participate in a voluntary job-training program. Of those who participated, only 14 percent were re-arrested within two years of release, compared with 29 percent of inmates who did not participate. Officials conclude that the program probably reduces re-arrest rates by giving former inmates marketable skills.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the officials' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Among program participants who were re-arrested, most had failed to complete the full training curriculum.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The program is funded primarily by a grant from the state's Department of Corrections.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Program participants who found employment within six months of release had re-arrest rates below 5 percent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants and non-participants had similar criminal histories and demographic profiles before entering the program.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Among inmates serving post-conviction sentences, those who participated in a similar program also had lower re-arrest rates.

explanations.correct: The comparison between participants and non-participants is only meaningful if they were similar to begin with. (D) rules out the alternative that participants were already less likely to re-offend, making the causal claim substantially more plausible.
explanations.A: If anything, weakens — it suggests completion rather than mere enrollment matters, which the officials' conclusion doesn't track.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — the funding source has no bearing on whether the program reduces re-arrest.
explanations.C: Tempting but introduces a different causal mechanism (employment), which the officials didn't claim.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Strengthens a different conclusion — about post-conviction inmates, not the pretrial population at issue.

difficultyReason: Rules out an alternative cause in an environmental argument. Trap (C) is the opposite answer; trap (A) strengthens a sister claim about a different wetland.
stimulus: Since the installation of a new filtration system at the textile plant upstream, the concentration of heavy metals in the Prellan wetlands has dropped by more than half. Researchers at the regional ecological institute conclude that the filtration system is probably responsible for the improved water quality.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A wetland thirty kilometers downstream from a similar textile plant has also shown declining heavy metal concentrations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heavy metals tend to bind to sediment, which is periodically flushed from wetlands during seasonal floods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other industrial facilities along the river reduced their output during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The textile plant's owners have publicly committed to installing similar systems at their other facilities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rainfall in the Prellan watershed during the year after the system's installation was consistent with the long-term average.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that unusual rainfall diluted the wetland's metal concentrations. (E) rules out that alternative, making the filtration system the more plausible cause of the observed drop.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about another wetland and another plant, not the Prellan causal claim.
explanations.B: Opposite answer — suggests a natural flushing mechanism that could account for the improvement.
explanations.C: Opposite answer — introduces an alternative cause (the other facilities) that could explain the drop independently of the filtration system.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — future commitments don't bear on past water quality.
explanations.E: Correct.

difficultyReason: Confirms a load-bearing premise in a technological argument. Trap (B) is an unwarranted comparison; trap (E) strengthens a neighboring claim about security rather than accuracy.
stimulus: A new machine-learning system for reading chest X-rays detected early-stage lung cancer in 92 percent of cases in its training dataset, compared with 78 percent for board-certified radiologists. The system's developers conclude that deploying the system at clinical sites will probably improve early cancer detection for actual patients.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a recent trial at three hospitals unaffiliated with the developers, the system correctly identified early-stage lung cancer in 90 percent of X-rays.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Radiologists who use an older decision-support tool tend to detect cancer slightly more often than those who do not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The system produces a visual heatmap highlighting regions of the X-ray it considers suspicious.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The developers hold several patents on machine-learning architectures for medical imaging.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The system has been certified by regulators as meeting current standards for patient data security.

explanations.correct: The developers' leap is from training-dataset accuracy to clinical performance. (A) confirms the key premise that the system generalizes to unfamiliar patients at unfamiliar sites, which is exactly what a deployment argument requires.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison — introduces a different tool with a different performance profile, without anchoring the new system's clinical prospects.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant to whether the system's detection rate will hold in clinical practice.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — patents don't speak to diagnostic accuracy.
explanations.E: Strengthens a different conclusion — about data security, not detection performance.

difficultyReason: Confirms a methodological assumption in a linguistic argument. Trap (E) is a plausible-sounding alternative cause; trap (B) strengthens a claim about reading comprehension, not vocabulary acquisition.
stimulus: Researchers tested two groups of adult learners of Spanish. Group A studied new vocabulary using spaced repetition flashcards over six weeks; Group B studied the same vocabulary by rereading passages containing the words. On a retention test given three months later, Group A recalled significantly more vocabulary than Group B. The researchers conclude that spaced repetition is probably a more effective long-term vocabulary study method than rereading.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Group A participants reported spending slightly less total time studying than Group B participants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both groups showed comparable gains on a reading-comprehension test given at the end of the six-week study period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spaced repetition has been shown to improve retention of mathematical formulas in a separate study of secondary-school students.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Before the study, the two groups scored similarly on a baseline Spanish vocabulary test.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Group A used mobile apps for their flashcards, while Group B used printed passages.

explanations.correct: The researchers' comparison assumes the two groups were starting from comparable Spanish knowledge. (D) confirms that assumption, ruling out the alternative that Group A simply knew more Spanish to begin with.
explanations.A: Tempting but ambiguous — the conclusion is about method effectiveness, not efficiency, and less total study time could equally cut against Group A's retention.
explanations.B: Strengthens a different conclusion — about reading comprehension rather than long-term vocabulary retention.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — extends to a different subject and a different population.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause — a format difference (apps vs. print) that could independently explain the retention gap.

difficultyReason: Rules out an alternative explanation in a historical argument. Trap (C) is accurate but irrelevant; trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion about a later period.
stimulus: Historians have long debated why grain prices in the Roman province of Egypt fell sharply during the reign of Emperor Trajan. One historian has recently argued that the decline was driven by Trajan's construction of new irrigation canals, which increased the amount of land under cultivation. Tax records from the period show a substantial rise in grain shipments from Egyptian ports.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most supports the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grain prices in Egypt rose again within a generation after Trajan's death.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Papyrus records indicate that many Egyptian landowners opposed the canal projects as disruptive to existing estates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trajan also commissioned major building projects in Rome, including a new forum and market complex.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some of the new canals were constructed by reusing materials from older, abandoned irrigation networks.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The province's population did not grow substantially during Trajan's reign, so demand for grain remained steady.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative explanation for falling prices is declining demand. (E) rules that out by showing demand was steady, leaving the supply-side explanation (more cultivated land from canals) as the more plausible cause.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about a later period and reversal, which doesn't bear on why prices fell under Trajan.
explanations.B: If anything, weakens — landowner opposition suggests the canal plan may have been less effective than assumed.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — building projects in Rome don't address Egyptian grain prices.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant to whether the canals increased cultivable land.
explanations.E: Correct.

difficultyReason: Confirms a premise about cause and effect in a policy argument. Trap (D) is the opposite answer; trap (E) is accurate but irrelevant.
stimulus: City planner: Since the Oakridge district installed protected bicycle lanes along its main commercial street two years ago, the number of cyclists using that street has doubled, while the number of reported collisions between cyclists and motor vehicles has fallen by 40 percent. The city council should conclude that installing similar protected lanes elsewhere would probably make cycling safer in those areas as well.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Oakridge district has a younger population on average than other districts in the city.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oakridge residents reported feeling safer walking on their commercial street after the lanes were installed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protected lanes in other cities of comparable size have produced similar reductions in cyclist-vehicle collisions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Motor vehicle traffic on Oakridge's main commercial street fell by 25 percent over the same two-year period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The protected lanes in Oakridge were funded by a federal transportation grant.

explanations.correct: The planner extrapolates from Oakridge to other districts. (C) confirms that protected lanes produce similar effects in comparable settings, shoring up the analogical leap to 'other areas.'
explanations.A: Introduces an alternative cause — younger populations could cycle more safely independently of the lanes, weakening the causal claim.
explanations.B: Strengthens a different conclusion — about pedestrian safety, not cyclist safety.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Opposite answer — fewer cars could independently explain fewer collisions, undermining the claim that the lanes themselves made cycling safer.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — funding source has no bearing on the safety effect.

difficultyReason: Confirms a premise about audience response in an arts argument. Trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion about ticket revenue; trap (E) is an alternative-cause distractor.
stimulus: Theater critic: The Midvale Playhouse's decision to stage shorter, ninety-minute productions rather than its traditional three-hour offerings has been a success. Subscription renewals have risen for three consecutive seasons, reversing a long decline. The playhouse should continue this shorter format to sustain audience loyalty.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In subscriber surveys, renewing patrons most often cite the shorter running time as the reason they continued their subscriptions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Individual ticket sales at the playhouse have also increased since the shorter productions began.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A neighboring theater that kept its traditional format has seen flat subscription numbers over the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ninety-minute productions have become more common among regional theaters nationwide.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The playhouse hired a new artistic director in the same season it introduced the shorter format.

explanations.correct: The critic attributes rising renewals to the shorter format. (A) confirms that patrons themselves credit the shorter running time, directly tying the cited effect to the proposed cause.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Strengthens a different conclusion — about overall revenue, not about whether the shorter format is driving subscriber loyalty.
explanations.C: Accurate but weak as support — the neighboring theater's flatness has many possible causes and doesn't pin the renewal rise on format specifically.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — national trends don't establish Midvale causation.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause — the new artistic director could be the real driver of renewal gains.

difficultyReason: Rules out an alternative cause in a medical prevention argument. Trap (D) is plausible support but strengthens a different population's claim; trap (B) is accurate but irrelevant.
stimulus: A cardiologist observed that her patients who had been taking a daily low-dose aspirin for at least five years were less likely to have a first heart attack than those who had not taken aspirin. She concluded that daily low-dose aspirin probably reduces the risk of a first heart attack.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the cardiologist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspirin is inexpensive and widely available without a prescription.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients taking daily aspirin also reported lower incidences of common headaches.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients in the two groups had similar rates of smoking, hypertension, and family history of heart disease.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Among patients who had already suffered one heart attack, those who took daily aspirin had fewer subsequent heart attacks.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Daily aspirin has been linked in other studies to a slightly increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.

explanations.correct: A reader should suspect that aspirin takers are simply healthier or more risk-averse to begin with. (C) rules out that alternative by equalizing the groups on key cardiac risk factors, isolating aspirin as the plausible cause.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant to whether aspirin reduces risk.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — headache rates don't bear on first-heart-attack risk.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about recurrent rather than first heart attacks.
explanations.E: If anything, weakens, by suggesting a countervailing harm.

difficultyReason: Bolsters an ethical argument by confirming an unstated empirical assumption. Trap (A) is accurate but irrelevant to the moral claim; trap (C) strengthens a different, more permissive conclusion.
stimulus: Ethicist: Animal welfare advocates argue that factory farming is unethical because it causes substantial suffering to farm animals. Some philosophers reply that this suffering is ethically insignificant because farm animals such as chickens and pigs lack the cognitive capacity for suffering in any morally relevant sense. But this reply is probably mistaken, and advocates are right to criticize the practice.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neuroscientific studies have shown that chickens and pigs possess brain structures that mediate pain experience in much the same way as those of species whose suffering is widely recognized as morally significant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factory-farmed meat is generally cheaper for consumers than meat from smaller, non-industrial farms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some philosophers hold that even animals that clearly can suffer may permissibly be killed for food under humane conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several countries have enacted laws restricting certain factory-farming practices, citing animal-welfare concerns.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Consumer surveys indicate that most meat buyers prefer not to think about the conditions under which farm animals are raised.

explanations.correct: The ethicist must rebut the philosophers' empirical premise that chickens and pigs lack the capacity for morally relevant suffering. (A) directly undercuts that premise with neuroscientific evidence, making the ethicist's conclusion more likely.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — price doesn't speak to the moral question at issue.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion — one that permits humane killing, which is not the ethicist's claim.
explanations.D: Accurate but weak support — legal enactments reflect opinion rather than settle the philosophical dispute.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — consumer psychology doesn't bear on the moral status of the animals.

difficultyReason: Closes an analogical gap in a legal argument. Trap (C) strengthens a neighboring claim about appellate review; trap (E) is accurate but irrelevant.
stimulus: Defense attorney: My client was convicted largely on testimony from a single eyewitness who identified him in a lineup conducted under poor lighting and considerable stress. Courts in this jurisdiction have overturned convictions in at least three comparable cases where a single stressed eyewitness's identification was the central evidence. The appellate court should therefore probably overturn my client's conviction.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most supports the defense attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The prosecutor who tried the client's case has a higher-than-average conviction rate in this jurisdiction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The client has maintained his innocence consistently throughout the trial and subsequent appeals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The appellate court has overturned convictions in several cases involving improper jury instructions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In each of the three overturned cases, the appellate court cited research showing that stress and poor lighting substantially reduce eyewitness accuracy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The client has no prior criminal record in this or any other jurisdiction.

explanations.correct: The attorney's argument relies on the analogy between this case and the three overturned cases. (D) confirms the ground of that analogy — that the same features (stress, poor lighting) were the basis for overturning — making the comparison much stronger.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — the prosecutor's record doesn't bear on appellate reversal.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — a defendant's protestations don't affect appellate standards.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion — about jury-instruction reversals, not eyewitness-based reversals.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant to whether the eyewitness identification is legally adequate.

difficultyReason: Confirms a mechanism in an environmental argument. Trap (A) is the opposite answer; trap (D) strengthens a different conclusion about a distinct species.
stimulus: After the state banned the use of a common agricultural pesticide, the population of the tricolor skipper butterfly in nearby meadows rose sharply for the first time in a decade. Entomologists conclude that the pesticide had probably been suppressing the butterfly's population.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the entomologists' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some farmers who had used the banned pesticide have switched to alternatives that entomologists consider less harmful to pollinators.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monarch butterfly populations in the same region also increased after the ban took effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Weather conditions in the meadows during the year of the ban were similar to those in earlier years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Laboratory tests show that even trace amounts of the banned pesticide are lethal to tricolor skipper larvae.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The banned pesticide had been marketed primarily as a treatment for aphids and other insect pests.

explanations.correct: The entomologists posit that the pesticide suppressed the butterflies. (D) supplies a mechanism — lethality to larvae at trace doses — that directly connects the pesticide to population suppression.
explanations.A: Opposite answer — if alternatives are in use, some of the new chemicals (not just the ban) could be affecting the population.
explanations.B: Strengthens a different conclusion — about a different species, suggesting at most a general effect rather than anchoring the tricolor skipper claim.
explanations.C: Helpful but weaker: rules out one alternative (weather) but doesn't tie the pesticide to the effect the way a mechanism does.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — the pesticide's marketed target doesn't establish its effect on butterflies.

difficultyReason: Rules out an alternative explanation in a technology-adoption argument. Trap (B) is accurate but irrelevant; trap (E) strengthens a different conclusion about a different demographic.
stimulus: A regional bank introduced a new mobile app last spring and found that customers who installed the app visit branch offices 30 percent less often than customers who have not installed it. The bank's chief executive concluded that the app is probably reducing customers' need to visit branches in person.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the executive's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Before installing the app, the two groups of customers visited branch offices at nearly identical rates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The app received generally positive reviews in several consumer technology publications.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bank reduced the opening hours of several branch offices shortly after releasing the app.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The app was developed jointly with a software firm that has built similar apps for other banks.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Among customers under 30, app installers visit branch offices considerably less than non-installers.

explanations.correct: A critical reader suspects that app installers were already less branch-dependent. (A) rules out that selection-effect alternative by showing the two groups had the same visit rate before the app existed.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — reviews don't establish that the app is reducing in-person visits.
explanations.C: Opposite answer — shorter hours could independently explain fewer visits, weakening the causal attribution to the app.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — the app's development history doesn't bear on its causal effect.
explanations.E: Strengthens a different conclusion — about under-30 customers specifically, rather than the overall customer base.

difficultyReason: Confirms a premise about causal direction in a linguistics argument. Trap (C) is an unwarranted comparison; trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion about a different contact situation.
stimulus: Linguist: Over the past three centuries, the English spoken in the coastal town of Hadrell has acquired a number of distinctive vowel pronunciations not found in neighboring towns. Hadrell historically hosted a large community of Dutch sailors, and the distinctive vowels closely resemble those of seventeenth-century Dutch. The distinctive vowels in Hadrell English probably originated through contact with Dutch speakers.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In another English port that hosted French-speaking sailors, English developed several borrowed vocabulary items from French.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The distinctive vowel pronunciations first appear in Hadrell written records only after Dutch sailors had been settling there for several decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The dialect spoken in a coastal town two hundred miles from Hadrell shares some lexical items with Dutch.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hadrell residents remain proud of their town's maritime heritage and often display Dutch-language signs at local festivals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seventeenth-century Dutch itself underwent vowel changes that distinguished it from earlier Dutch dialects.

explanations.correct: The argument needs the distinctive vowels to come from Dutch contact, not to predate it. (B) establishes the causal timing — the vowels emerged after Dutch sailors arrived — which strongly supports Dutch-to-English transmission.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about a different town and vocabulary rather than vowels in Hadrell.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — a separate town with different contact conditions doesn't support the Hadrell claim.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — modern pride doesn't establish historical linguistic transmission.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — internal Dutch history doesn't show that Hadrell English borrowed from it.

difficultyReason: Confirms a causal mechanism in a historical argument. Trap (D) is the opposite answer; trap (B) is accurate but irrelevant to the specific causal claim.
stimulus: Historian: Why did the Verran Republic collapse in 1783? One traditional account blames a crop failure that year. I suspect, instead, that the collapse was driven primarily by the republic's decision a decade earlier to devalue its currency, which drove foreign creditors to withdraw investment in the years that followed. Tax receipts from the republic's port cities had been shrinking steadily since the devaluation.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several contemporary pamphleteers in the republic blamed the collapse on an incompetent military.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Verran Republic had experienced two earlier currency devaluations in the previous century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Records show that foreign creditors pulled nearly two-thirds of their investments from Verran ventures in the years between the devaluation and the collapse.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1783 crop failure was among the most severe the republic had recorded in its history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neighboring republics that did not devalue their currency experienced modest growth during the same decade.

explanations.correct: The historian's chain runs from devaluation to creditor withdrawal to collapse. (C) directly confirms the crucial middle link — that creditors did in fact pull out on a large scale — making the causal chain substantially more credible.
explanations.A: Introduces a third explanation (military incompetence) that doesn't bear on devaluation vs. crop failure.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — earlier devaluations don't bear on whether this one caused the collapse.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Opposite answer — a severe crop failure makes the traditional crop-failure account more plausible, undermining the historian.
explanations.E: Weak support: speaks generally to devaluation's effects but doesn't tie withdrawal to the Verran collapse specifically.

difficultyReason: Closes an analogical gap in a public-policy argument. Trap (A) strengthens a different claim about fiscal cost; trap (E) is accurate but irrelevant to educational outcomes.
stimulus: Education policy advisor: The Nortongate school district saw substantial gains in elementary reading scores after adopting a phonics-focused curriculum two years ago. The neighboring Westfell district is now considering the same curriculum and should probably expect similar gains in its own elementary reading scores.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the advisor's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Implementing the phonics-focused curriculum in Nortongate cost less than the district's previous reading program.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nortongate and Westfell have comparable class sizes, teacher-experience distributions, and student demographics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reading scores across the state have risen modestly over the past five years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Westfell's teachers have expressed concern about the time required to retrain for a new curriculum.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nortongate voters recently approved additional bond funding for school library resources.

explanations.correct: The advisor extrapolates from one district to another. (B) confirms the relevant similarities between the districts, tightening the analogy and making comparable gains more likely.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about cost rather than about reading-score gains.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite answer — a statewide rise could independently explain Nortongate's gains, weakening the attribution to the curriculum.
explanations.D: If anything, weakens — teacher resistance could undermine implementation in Westfell.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause — extra library funding, not the phonics curriculum, may have driven Nortongate's gains.

difficultyReason: Confirms a premise about artistic influence. Trap (E) is accurate but irrelevant; trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion about a later period.
stimulus: Art historian: Several compositions in the early works of the painter Ilse Krevel — particularly the use of foreground lanterns to frame crowds — closely parallel compositions in the etchings of the seventeenth-century Dutch printmaker Adriaen van Ostade. Although Krevel never acknowledged van Ostade as an influence, her early compositions were probably shaped by familiarity with his work.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Krevel's late paintings abandoned lantern-framing compositions in favor of flatter, more diffuse lighting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Krevel spent the two years before painting her earliest works as a student at an academy whose library held a well-used collection of van Ostade etchings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Van Ostade's etchings were reprinted in inexpensive editions during the twentieth century and were widely available to art students in Krevel's era.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other painters of Krevel's generation have been shown to have drawn on seventeenth-century Dutch printmakers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Krevel's later critical writings describe van Ostade's work in generally dismissive terms.

explanations.correct: The argument depends on Krevel having been familiar with van Ostade before painting her early works. (B) specifically places van Ostade's etchings in her study environment just before the relevant paintings, directly supporting the familiarity premise.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about her late style rather than the early compositions the historian concerns.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Weaker support — general availability doesn't establish Krevel's own familiarity the way documented access does.
explanations.D: Accurate but weak — what other painters did doesn't show what Krevel did.
explanations.E: If anything, weakens, by suggesting Krevel was unfamiliar with or uninterested in van Ostade.

difficultyReason: Rules out an alternative cause in an economic argument. Trap (C) is an unwarranted comparison; trap (D) strengthens a different conclusion about a related but distinct industry.
stimulus: Last year, online retailer Parvest doubled the number of fulfillment warehouses serving its largest metropolitan market. Average delivery times for Parvest orders in that market have since fallen from 48 hours to 22 hours. The company's operations director concluded that the additional warehouses are probably responsible for the faster deliveries.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parvest hired a new chief logistics officer three months before the warehouses opened.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Order volume in the metropolitan market did not change appreciably before or after the warehouses opened.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A competing retailer that did not add warehouses also saw its delivery times improve, but by a smaller margin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parvest's grocery subsidiary, which uses a separate distribution network, has also seen faster deliveries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The new warehouses are located closer, on average, to the neighborhoods receiving the most Parvest orders.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that order volume changed in a way that eased the existing network (fewer orders would shorten times even without new warehouses). (B) rules that out, making the new warehouses the more plausible cause of faster delivery.
explanations.A: Introduces an alternative cause — the new logistics officer could have implemented other changes responsible for faster delivery.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — a competitor's improvement suggests industry-wide factors and doesn't isolate the warehouses.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about the grocery subsidiary's separate network.
explanations.E: Tempting, but closer-to-customer proximity largely restates what adding warehouses accomplishes; without ruling out alternative causes such as a volume change, it doesn't anchor the causal claim as directly as (B).
